knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
source("inventory_auction.R")

## The decision

A buyer sells one unit when demand arrives and can buy at most one unit in
each auction. A purchase can serve today's demand or remain in inventory
for a later period. Entering an auction costs a fixed fee, whether or not
the buyer wins.

The highest rival bid is an exogenous random threshold. If the buyer bids
at least this threshold, it wins and pays the threshold. Rival bids do not
respond to the buyer's inventory or policy. This is a single-agent
inventory problem with auction purchases; it does not solve a dynamic
equilibrium among bidders.

All quantities below are chosen for this exercise. They are not estimates
from an industry dataset.

## Timing and Bellman equation

1. Observe beginning inventory $s \in \{0,1,2,3\}$.
2. Choose a bid $b \in \{0,0.5,1,1.5,2\}$. Zero means no participation.
3. Draw the rival-bid threshold $z$ and execute the purchase. Let
   $w=\mathbf{1}\{b>0,\ z\le b\}$.
4. Draw demand $d\in\{0,1\}$. Serve $y=\min(s+w,d)$ and carry
   $s'=s+w-y$ into the next period.

A full inventory permits only no participation, so the capacity constraint
also holds before demand is realized. Thresholds and demand are independent
across periods and independent of one another. Ties with the threshold are
won by the buyer.

With sales revenue $m$, entry fee $k$, holding cost $h$, and discount factor
$\delta$, the Bellman equation is

$$
V(s)=\max_{b\in B(s)}\mathbb{E}_{z,d}
\left[m y-z w-k\mathbf{1}\{b>0\}-h s'+\delta V(s')\right].
$$

The threshold has equal probability on $\{0.25,0.75,1.25,1.75\}$.
Demand arrives with probability $0.6$. The baseline uses $m=2.4$, $k=0.08$,
$h=0.08$, and $\delta=0.95$. The expectation is calculated by enumerating
every threshold-demand combination; there is no simulation error in the
Bellman calculation. Bids remain restricted to the stated finite grid.

## Solve and check the policy

```{r solve}
model <- inventory_model()
fit <- solve_inventory(model)
myopic_model <- model
myopic_model$discount <- 0
myopic <- solve_inventory(myopic_model)
knitr::kable(data.frame(inventory = model$states,
                       dynamic_bid = fit$bid, myopic_bid = myopic$bid))
fit$residual
fit$error_bound
```

The reported residual is $\|T V-V\|_\infty$. Since $T$ is a contraction,
the value-function error is bounded by the residual divided by
$1-\delta$. This bounds numerical solution error for this finite model;
it does not bound error from the bid grid or the economic assumptions.

## Compare simulated paths

The next calculation uses 30 independent replications, each with 200 burn-in
periods followed by 2,000 measured periods. Within each replication all
policies face the same threshold and demand draws. The myopic policy
maximizes current profit and ignores continuation value. The third policy
never participates and starts with empty inventory.

```{r compare}
result_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "inventory-auction")
results <- run_inventory_example(result_dir, verbose = FALSE)
knitr::kable(results$summary, digits = 4)
knitr::kable(results$comparison, digits = 4)
```

```{r figure, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(result_dir, "inventory-auction.png"), rel_path = FALSE)
```

Error bars are 95% t intervals for the mean simulated profit across
replications. The paired comparison uses the profit difference within
each replication. These intervals describe Monte Carlo uncertainty under
the stated model. Long-run simulated average profit is a separate metric
from the discounted objective used to choose the dynamic policy.

## Exercises

1. Change the entry fee and holding cost separately. Report the full policy
   table and participation rate; do not infer a general monotonicity result
   from one parameter setting.
2. Refine the bid grid and compare values and policies at each inventory
   level. Explain why changing the grid can change the policy even when
   the Bellman residual is small.
3. Replace the independent rival thresholds with a persistent price state.
   Specify what the buyer observes before bidding and include that state
   in the transition law.

The example connects the repository's auction chapter and single-agent
dynamic decision chapter. The base R script runs independently of the
course package and does not change the assessed assignments.
